faqs.question: What are good Halloween costume party ideas?
faqs.answer: Start with the costume rule rather than the décor: pick one of four dress codes, from costume required to costume optional, and one theme that sets a clear rule, such as dressing as your first initial. Then add a fair contest, a costume box by the door for anyone who forgot, and a line-up photo straight after the vote.

faqs.question: What are some costume party themes that aren't just decorations?
faqs.answer: Themes that set a costume rule work in any room: initial night, a colour draw texted a week ahead, the job you never had, a one-prop party, blind pairs who plan by message, and dress-at-the-door from a shared box. Each one gives judges something specific to reward.

faqs.question: What does costume optional mean on a party invite?
faqs.answer: It means guests can come in normal clothes without feeling out of place. Mention that spares are waiting by the door, and skip a big prize contest, because guests who did not dress up would only watch it.

faqs.question: How do you judge a Halloween costume contest fairly?
faqs.answer: Announce the criteria in the invite, hold one parade so everyone sees every costume, and vote only afterwards. A 2017 study of song contests found judges ranked later performers higher even when the order was random, so voting as people arrive favours latecomers.

faqs.question: What is the fairest way for guests to vote on costumes?
faqs.answer: An approval ballot: each guest gets a numbered card and ticks every costume they like, and the highest tally takes the prize. A vote for a friend no longer blocks a vote for the best outfit, though ties are more likely, so plan a 10-second cheer as the tie-break.

faqs.question: What categories should a costume contest have?
faqs.answer: Three is enough for about 20 guests: best fit to the theme rule, best costume built from the costume box, and best pair or group. Let nobody win twice so prizes spread around the room.

faqs.question: What are good prizes for a Halloween costume contest?
faqs.answer: Small ones work: a rosette, first pick of the sweet bowl, or control of the playlist for three songs, at roughly $5 to $15 each as an estimate. The vote matters more to most guests than the prize.

faqs.question: What should I do if a guest arrives without a costume?
faqs.answer: Hand them the costume box: ears, a cape, stick-on moustaches or a face-paint palette sold for skin use gets them dressed within about 5 minutes. A guest who would rather stay in plain clothes can be guest judge instead.

faqs.question: How do I ask guests to avoid culturally offensive costumes?
faqs.answer: Add one plain line to the invite, such as asking for characters, creatures and puns rather than other people's cultures and faiths. York University's Centre for Human Rights suggests checking whether a costume plays on a stereotype, copies a sacred or cultural garment, revives a discriminatory look or packages a cultural practice for sale.

faqs.question: How can a guest in a wheelchair take part in a costume contest?
faqs.answer: Judge the costume, not how easily the wearer moves in it, and run the parade on one level. The chair can be the centre of the idea: the US nonprofit Magic Wheelchair builds whole costumes around wheelchairs.

faqs.question: When should I hold a Halloween costume party in 2026 and 2027?
faqs.answer: Halloween is on Saturday 31 October 2026, so the night itself works. In 2027 it falls on Sunday 31 October, so Saturday 30 October 2027 suits most guests.

faqs.question: Can SubhSandesh run my costume party invites or contest?
faqs.answer: No. SubhSandesh Halloween pages are one-person greeting pages with no RSVPs, ballots or guest lists. Use one afterwards for a single person, such as the contest winner or a friend who missed the party.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Halloween Costume Party Ideas: Dress Codes, Contests, Costume Box

The best Halloween costume party ideas are rules about costumes, not décor: one clear dress code, a contest guests trust, a box for anyone who turns up in jeans, and a check that no outfit borrows someone else's culture. Two SubhSandesh numbers shape that plan.

At Raksha Bandhan 2026, our nearest measured festival (n = 89 pages), 49.4% of pages were built on the day itself, so expect guests to settle on costumes late and give them a low minimum. And 48.3% of shared SubhSandesh pages are opened on a phone, so the contest photo will mostly be seen at thumbnail size.

Halloween falls on Saturday 31 October 2026 and Sunday 31 October 2027, so most parties land on Saturday 31 October 2026 or Saturday 30 October 2027. Below: four dress codes, six costume party themes, a fair contest, the costume box, inclusion checks and a photo plan.

## What makes a party a costume party?

A costume party is a gathering where dressing as someone or something else is the main event. The host sets the costume rule and makes it easy to follow.

In a [2013 PLOS ONE study by Novelli, Drury, Reicher and Stott](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC3827307), people who identified more with the crowd at a packed outdoor dance-music event (n = 48) felt less crowded and, through that, reported more positive emotion. It measured crowds, not parties, but a shared costume rule is a cheap way to bond 20 guests.

## Four dress codes, and the line that sets each

Choose the dress code before the theme, because it decides who feels underdressed at 9 pm. Each tier has a minimum and a line to paste into the invite.

**Tier 1: costume required, theme strict.** Minimum: a full outfit that obeys the theme rule. Suits 8 to 20 guests who already love dressing up.

- "Full costume, on theme. Half-built is fine; plain clothes are not."

**Tier 2: costume required, any character.** Minimum: anything clearly not your normal self.

- "Any costume counts. Arrive as yourself, leave as somebody else."

**Tier 3: costume encouraged.** Minimum: one piece, such as ears, a cape or a drawn-on moustache.

- "One costume piece is the minimum. Ten is the dream."

**Tier 4: costume optional.** Minimum: none, with the costume box as a quiet offer.

- "Dress up or come as you are. Spares wait in a box by the door."

Never pair Tier 4 with a big contest. Guests who skipped costumes would watch the prizes from the sofa.

## Six costume party themes that each set one rule

Each theme is a costume rule, not a décor scheme, so it works in a flat or a hired hall. Entries give the rule, who it suits, estimated spend per guest (EST, USD) and what judges reward.

### 1. Initial night

- **Rule:** dress as something that starts with your first initial.
- **Suits:** 10 to 30 guests who half-know each other; names stick.
- **EST spend:** $0–15.
- **Judges reward:** the most unexpected match to the letter.

### 2. Colour draw

- **Rule:** a week ahead, text each guest one colour; their character must be mostly that colour.
- **Suits:** 12 to 24 guests; the group photo looks planned.
- **EST spend:** $5–20.
- **Judges reward:** full commitment, from shoes to make-up.

### 3. The job you never had

- **Rule:** dress as a job you have never done, carrying one tool of that trade.
- **Suits:** adults and mixed-age family parties.
- **EST spend:** $5–25.
- **Judges reward:** a stranger naming the job after one question.

### 4. One-prop party

- **Rule:** normal clothes plus one handheld prop that carries the whole character.
- **Suits:** costume-shy crowds, and guests who find fabric, heat or bulk hard.
- **EST spend:** $0–10.
- **Judges reward:** the prop that tells the most story.

### 5. Blind pairs

- **Rule:** the host secretly pairs near-strangers, who plan a joint costume by message.
- **Suits:** merging two friend groups; needs an even number, 10 to 20.
- **EST spend:** $5–20 each.
- **Judges reward:** the pair whose two halves only make sense together.

### 6. Dress at the door

- **Rule:** nobody arrives in costume; everyone builds one from the costume box in 10 minutes.
- **Suits:** same-week parties, teenagers and families.
- **EST spend:** $40–80 for the host's box; $0 for guests.
- **Judges reward:** the box costume nobody else could have made.

## How to run a fair costume contest

A fair contest announces its criteria in the invite and shows every costume before any vote. Score each entrant out of 10: fit to the theme rule 4, craft visible from one metre 2, staying in character 2, still intact at the vote 2. Pick three categories for 20 guests, and nobody wins twice:

- Best fit to the theme rule
- Best costume built from the box
- Best pair or group

In New Wave song contest data from 2005 to 2016, [Antipov and Pokryshevskaya (Judgment and Decision Making, July 2017)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/judgment-and-decision-making/article/order-effects-in-the-results-of-song-contests-evidence-from-the-eurovision-and-the-new-wave/C03D0D5AA384362736FE1EB59A75516C) found expert judges ranked later performers higher although the order was drawn at random; Eurovision finals from 2009 to 2012 gave weaker evidence. Experts were no less biased than televoters, so hold one parade and vote only after the last costume has passed.

An approval ballot is, in our view, the fairest party vote. Give each guest a card numbering every entrant and let them tick all they like, so a tick for a friend never blocks one for the best outfit.

Break ties with a 10-second cheer, judged by the one guest still in plain clothes. Prizes stay small, roughly $5–15 each (EST): a rosette, first pick of the sweet bowl, or control of the playlist for three songs.

Four ways to pick a winner, compared for a 20-guest party. Times are our estimates.

| Method | Best for | Time for 20 guests (EST) | Main fairness risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| Show of hands | Under 10 guests | 3 minutes | Loud friend groups decide it |
| Secret single vote | 10 to 30 guests | 8 minutes | Similar costumes split the vote |
| Approval ballot (tick all you like) | 10 to 40 guests | 10 minutes | More ties; plan a tie-break |
| Two judges with the 10-point score | Prizes worth over $20 | 15 minutes | Late entrants favoured unless one parade |

For most parties, the approval ballot leaves the least room for a popularity contest. Use hands only under 10 guests.

## The costume box: dressing guests who arrive without one

Keep one box by the door so the guest who forgot is in costume within 5 minutes and nobody is singled out. A starter box for 20 guests is about $40–80 (EST).

- 4 headbands with ears or horns, one size
- 2 knee-length capes, nothing that trails on the floor
- Stick-on moustaches and a pack of fresh make-up sponges
- A face-paint palette sold for skin use, with wipes
- A roll of masking tape and a pen for "I am: ___" labels
- Safety pins and two spare black T-shirts
- 4 reflective armbands for the walk home

No shared masks, and wipe headbands between wearers. A guest who will not dress up at all gets a role instead: guest judge, with a badge and the tie-break.

## Inclusive costumes: culture, mobility and the senses

York University's Centre for Human Rights published five costume questions on [26 October 2016](https://www.yorku.ca/yfile/?p=235669). In short: does it play on a stereotype of a race, culture or religion; copy a garment significant to a faith or culture you are not part of; revive a look now seen as discriminatory; or package a cultural practice for sale? A yes to any of those four means choose again; the fifth is a mirror test.

Put it in the invite as a single line. Longer rules read as accusations:

- "Characters, creatures and puns welcome. Other people's cultures and faiths are not costumes."

For guests who use a wheelchair, crutches or a walker, judge the costume, not the effort of moving in it. The US nonprofit [Magic Wheelchair](https://www.magicwheelchair.org/) builds full costumes around wheelchairs; at home, run the parade on one level.

The [National Autistic Society](https://www.autism.org.uk/advice-and-guidance/about-autism/sensory-processing) lists fabric textures, feeling too hot, loud music and unexpected noises among common sensory triggers, and advises telling people what to expect. So name the parade time, any fog machine and any strobe in the invite, keep a quiet room, and count a single prop as a full costume.

## The photo plan: booth, line-up and consent

Take one official line-up photo straight after the vote, while every costume is still intact. Shoot landscape at chest height, head to toe, because 48.3% of SubhSandesh pages are opened on a phone and the group shot will mostly be seen small.

Put the photo booth where the parade ends, so every costume passes it once. Ask before you post: a masked guest may have come precisely because nobody could tell it was them. 38.5% of SubhSandesh creators password-protect a page before sharing it, and an average page draws 11.1 views, so assume a posted photo is seen more than once by people who were not there.

## When a costume party is the wrong plan

Skip the costume rule if fewer than half your list enjoys dressing up, or if several guests avoid Halloween for faith reasons. A Tier 4 gathering with no contest is kinder.

SubhSandesh is not a party tool either. Our Halloween pages are one-person greeting pages, with no RSVPs, ballots or guest lists, so use one for a single person: the contest winner or the friend who missed it.

The [interactive Halloween card with a Boo License](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween) takes about 5 minutes and holds up to 6 photos; it ends in a 1080×1920 licence showing their photo in a costume you pick from eight, such as witch, mummy or black cat. The [premium Halloween page with a voice note](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween-premium) takes about 10 minutes and adds up to 60 seconds of your voice, up to 12 photos, an unlock time and one reply box. To ask one person to be your plus-one, the [date invitation page](https://subhsandesh.in/date-invitation) needs an answer, and a yes becomes a countdown.

## Sources

- Novelli et al., crowd identification and positive emotion, PLOS ONE, 13 November 2013.
- Antipov and Pokryshevskaya, song-contest order effects, Judgment and Decision Making, July 2017.
- York University Centre for Human Rights, 26 October 2016.
- National Autistic Society, sensory processing (undated).
- Magic Wheelchair homepage (undated).
- SubhSandesh first-party data, measured 24 September and 9 September 2026.

Crowd events, not parties.

Antipov and Pokryshevskaya, JDM 12(4), July 2017, pp. 415-419 (CC BY 3.0, full text read): in the New Wave contest 2005-2016 expert judgments were significantly influenced by randomly assigned running number (later = ranked higher); weaker evidence in Eurovision finals 2009-2012; no evidence experts were less affected than televoting.

York University Centre for Human Rights, posted 26 October 2016: five questions (stereotype or stigma of a race, culture or religion; replication of a garment significant to a religion or culture you do not identify with; historical look now considered offensive; cultural practice commoditised; mirror test). Yes to questions 1-4 means the costume has potential to cause harm.

Common hyper-sensitivity triggers include fabric textures (clothing), feeling too hot or cold, loud music and unexpected noises; general support strategies include telling the person what to expect beforehand and providing a safe space away from triggers. Page undated.

structuralLimitations: No Halloween usage data exists in facts.md; the late-decision line is Raksha Bandhan 2026 (n = 89), labelled in the body as our nearest measured festival.
SERP measured with WebSearch (US index), 1 search for the keyword plus 1 for the appropriation source (2 of 2 budget). thebash.com returned 403 (snippet only); howstuffworks returned empty content.

Europe PMC search API returned 503 and then failed DNS during research, so no costume/identity-play paper was found beyond the crowd-identity study; terms tried: 'costume wearing identity play adults', 'dressing up fancy dress festival identity', 'cosplay identity wellbeing', '"costume" "social identity"', 'deindividuation costume anonymity group'. Candidates found were Frontiers (banned) or off-subject.
Novelli et al. 2013 is PLOS ONE (megajournal); this makes PLOS ONE 2 posts in the batch (boo-grams is the other). Full text read on journals.plos.org; linked via Europe PMC.

SERP overlap with b1 halloween-party-themes: 0 of 10 URLs shared (its top 10 was spookylittlehalloween, reddit, juliacharles, pinterest x2, treschicparty, care.com, classpop, halloweenforum, 1800flowers), so no cannibalisation by URL; intent overlap on 'themes' handled by defining every theme as a costume rule, none of b1's 18 décor themes reused.
Voting-method times and prize/box costs are editorial estimates, labelled EST; no study measures party costume contests directly.

auditReport.honestAssessment: The top results (greenvelope, punchbowl, trybooking, mother.ly) are décor-and-theme lists that mention a contest in one line; this is the only page giving dress-code tiers with wording, a judging rubric, an approval ballot with a sourced order-effect reason to vote after one parade, a costed costume box and dated inclusion guidance. Those are concrete, citable mechanics an answer engine can lift, but the domain is far weaker than the incumbents and no first-party Halloween data exists, so expect months, not weeks, and no ranking is predicted.
